q: You type https://shop.example into the address bar and nothing is cached. In what order do these steps happen?
options: TCP connection, DNS lookup, TLS handshake, HTTP request
DNS lookup, TLS handshake, TCP connection, HTTP request
DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS handshake, HTTP request
DNS lookup, TCP connection, HTTP request, TLS handshake
why: The browser first needs the server's IP address (DNS) to know where to connect. Then it opens a TCP connection, runs TLS over it to set up encryption, and only then sends the HTTP request, so the request is already protected.
wrong: A TCP connection needs an IP address, and DNS is what turns the name into one.
TLS runs on top of an open TCP connection, so the connection has to exist first.
Sending the request before TLS would expose it in plain text. HTTPS encrypts before the first request.

q: The HTML of a page arrives. It refers to a stylesheet, a script and five images. What does the browser do next?
options: Nothing more: the server sends the referenced files right after the HTML on its own
It reads the HTML, finds those references and sends a request for each file
It waits and requests each image only when that image scrolls into view, never earlier
It opens a brand new DNS lookup and TCP connection for every single file
why: An HTML response holds markup and references, not the files themselves. As the browser parses it, it requests each stylesheet, script and image, usually reusing connections it already has to the same server.
wrong: In plain HTTP the server answers requests; the browser must ask for each referenced file by its URL.
Lazy loading exists but is opt-in per image; stylesheets and scripts are requested as soon as they are found.
Files on the same host can reuse an open connection, and the DNS answer is cached after the first lookup.

q: You type http://shop.example. The server answers 301 with Location: https://shop.example/. What happens next?
options: The browser shows an error, since a 3xx code means the request failed
The page is already inside the 301 response, so the browser just shows it
The browser switches the same port 80 connection to encrypted in place
The browser sends a new request to the https address, this time over TLS
why: A 301 says the resource lives at another URL for good. The browser follows the Location header and makes a new request there. An https URL means port 443 and a TLS handshake, so a new secure connection is set up.
wrong: 3xx codes are redirects, not failures. Errors are 4xx and 5xx.
A redirect response points elsewhere. The page itself comes from the follow-up request.
http and https normally use different ports (80 and 443). The browser opens a separate connection and runs TLS on it.

q: A page on https://shop.example has loaded. Seconds later the user clicks a link to another page on the same site. Why does the new request usually start faster?
options: The server remembers the user from the last request and skips its own work
It reuses the open connection, so DNS, TCP and TLS setup are skipped
The second page is served from the HTTP cache without contacting the server
The browser switches to UDP once a site is known, which avoids handshakes
why: Setting up a connection costs round trips: a DNS lookup, the TCP handshake and the TLS handshake. Browsers keep connections open for a while, so a request to the same host right after can go out at once on the existing one.
wrong: HTTP is stateless, so the server does not skip its work. The saving is in setup before the request.
This page was never fetched, so there is nothing cached to show. The request still goes to the server.
HTTP over TCP does not switch protocols per visit. The speedup comes from keeping the TCP and TLS connection open.

q: A user downloads a 2 GB installer. Why is this transfer done over TCP rather than UDP?
options: TCP is faster than UDP for every kind of traffic
TCP encrypts the bytes, so nobody can tamper with the installer
UDP cannot send anything larger than a single packet
Every byte must arrive, in order, and TCP resends what is lost
why: A file with one missing or swapped chunk is broken. TCP numbers the bytes, has the receiver acknowledge them, resends what is lost and hands the data to the app in order, so the program does not have to build that itself.
wrong: TCP's acknowledgements and resends add work. For loss-tolerant live data UDP often has lower delay.
TCP does not encrypt anything. That is TLS, which runs on top of TCP for HTTPS.
An app can split a file across many UDP packets. It would then have to rebuild ordering and resending itself.

q: Most video call apps send audio and video over UDP. What is the main reason?
options: A late audio packet is useless, so skipping it beats waiting for a resend
UDP keeps packets in the order they were sent, which smooth video depends on
UDP encrypts the stream by default, which keeps the call private
UDP does not lose packets as long as the network is fast enough
why: In a live call, sound that arrives half a second late is worse than a tiny gap. UDP delivers what it can with no resends and no waiting, and the app hides small losses. TCP would stall the stream to resend old data.
wrong: UDP gives no ordering guarantee. Apps add sequence numbers themselves when they need them.
UDP has no encryption. Calls are encrypted by protocols the app runs on top of it.
Any network can drop packets, fast or slow. UDP does not detect or fix that.

q: An upload over TCP is running when the Wi-Fi drops for several hours. What does TCP's "reliable delivery" mean in this situation?
options: The data waits inside the network and is delivered as soon as the Wi-Fi returns
TCP resends lost data for a while, then gives up and the app gets an error
Lost bytes are skipped so the upload still finishes, just with gaps
The OS saves the upload and resumes it on a new connection by itself
why: Reliable means TCP detects loss through missing acknowledgements and resends while the path might come back. It cannot deliver over a dead network: after enough failed tries the connection breaks and the program sees an error it must handle.
wrong: Routers do not hold your data for minutes. Unacknowledged data stays with the sender, which keeps retrying.
TCP never hands over a stream with holes. Skipping lost data is UDP-style behaviour.
Resuming on a new connection is the application's job, for example by asking the server which bytes it has.

q: On one TCP connection the sender writes "AB" and then "CD". The packet with CD arrives before the packet with AB. What does the receiving program read?
options: CDAB, because data is handed over in arrival order
Only CD, because the late packet with AB is thrown away
ABCD, because TCP holds CD back until AB has arrived
Two separate messages that the program must sort by number
why: TCP numbers every byte. When later bytes arrive early, the receiver keeps them in a buffer and passes data to the program only in the original order, so it reads ABCD.
wrong: Putting data back in order is one of TCP's core jobs. The program never sees arrival order.
A late packet is not a duplicate. TCP accepts it and fills the gap.
TCP gives the program a single ordered stream of bytes, with no message boundaries and nothing to sort.

q: A multiplayer game sends player positions over TCP 30 times a second. When a packet is lost, other players freeze for a moment and then jump. What causes this?
options: TCP opens a new connection with a handshake for every position update
Routers always serve UDP first, so TCP packets wait in their queues
TCP encrypts each packet, and the extra work delays every update
TCP delivers in order, so one lost packet holds back newer updates
why: The receiver cannot see any data after a gap until the lost packet is resent, even though the newer positions have already arrived and make the old one useless. That wait is head-of-line blocking, and it is why games often use UDP and just keep the latest update.
wrong: One TCP connection carries all the updates. The handshake happens once, at the start.
Routers do not give UDP priority by default. The delay is caused by TCP's own ordering.
TCP itself has no encryption. And a constant cost would not cause sudden freezes.

q: Opening shop.example fails at once and the server logs show no request at all, yet the same site loads when you type its IP address. Which step failed?
options: The server returned 404 because the page does not exist
Turning the hostname into an IP address (DNS)
The server crashed while it was building the page
The TLS certificate check found an invalid certificate
why: Before the browser can connect it asks DNS for the IP address behind the name. Here that lookup gave no answer, so no connection was even attempted. A typo in the name or a broken resolver are common causes.
wrong: A 404 is a reply from the server, so DNS and the connection must have worked already.
A crash would show as a 5xx code or a dropped connection, which both need the address first.
The certificate is checked during TLS, after the browser has found and connected to the server.

q: You move a site to a new server and point its DNS record at the new IP. For a few hours some users still reach the old server. Why?
options: Resolvers cached the old answer and keep using it until its TTL runs out
DNS records around the world are only refreshed once a day, at midnight
Their browsers cached the HTML, and the IP address is stored inside it
Routers on the Internet route by domain name and need hours to relearn it
why: Each DNS answer comes with a TTL saying how long it may be cached. Resolvers, the OS and the browser reuse the old IP until that time passes. Lowering the TTL a day before a move makes the switch quicker.
wrong: There is no global refresh time. Each cached answer expires on its own TTL.
HTML does not contain the server's IP. The browser looks the name up through DNS.
Routers forward by IP address only. Names are turned into addresses by DNS before any packet is sent.

q: Why do most DNS lookups use UDP instead of TCP?
options: DNS answers are not very important, so losing a few now and then is acceptable
Each query and answer fits in one packet, so a handshake only adds delay
UDP hides the looked-up name from anyone watching the network
TCP cannot carry DNS messages at all, so UDP is the only choice
why: A lookup is one short question and one short answer. A TCP handshake would cost an extra round trip before that. With UDP the resolver just sends the query and, if no answer comes back in time, asks again.
wrong: Lookups matter a lot. A lost one is simply sent again after a timeout.
UDP has no encryption. Plain DNS queries can be read by anyone on the path.
DNS also runs over TCP, for example when an answer is too large for one UDP message.

q: A login form sends the username and password. Why should it use POST rather than GET?
options: POST encrypts the request body, while GET sends everything in plain text
GET has no way to send any data to the server at all
GET puts the fields in the URL, which ends up in history and logs
Servers process POST requests faster than GET requests
why: With GET, form fields become the query string of the URL. URLs are saved in browser history, server and proxy logs and bookmarks, so the password would be stored in many places. POST sends the fields in the request body.
wrong: Neither method encrypts anything. Only HTTPS does, and it protects GET and POST alike.
GET sends data in the URL's query string. That is exactly the problem here.
Speed is not the difference. The methods differ in meaning and in where the data travels.

q: An admin page deletes an item when its link GET /items/5/delete is followed. Items vanish though the admin clicked nothing, and the logs show the browser prefetching links. Which rule was broken?
options: GET requests must never carry cookies or other login data
GET should be safe: it should not change data on the server
Deleting data is only allowed over a connection that uses HTTPS
A delete must answer 204 No Content, never 200 OK
why: Browsers, crawlers and link previews assume GET only reads, so they fetch links freely. Putting a delete behind GET means any of them can trigger it. A state change belongs in DELETE or POST, which these tools do not send on their own.
wrong: GET requests normally do carry cookies. That is how pages know who is logged in.
HTTPS protects the data in transit. It does not stop a prefetch from following the link.
The status code is not the issue. The problem is that a read method changes data.

q: A mobile app's request times out, and the app cannot tell whether the server handled it. Which request can it simply send again without risking a doubled effect?
options: PUT /users/7/email with the new address
PATCH /accounts/7 with {"addCredit": 10}
POST /orders with the contents of the cart
Any of these: HTTP drops repeated requests by itself
why: PUT sets a resource to a given value, so doing it twice leaves the same state as doing it once: it is idempotent. Repeating a POST that creates something, or a change that adds an amount, applies the effect twice.
wrong: Adding 10 twice gives 20. A change that is relative to the current value is not idempotent.
Each POST /orders may create one more order, so a retry can place a duplicate order.
HTTP has no built-in duplicate detection. APIs add idempotency keys when POST must be safe to retry.

q: DELETE /items/9 returns 204. The client missed the reply and sends the same DELETE again, which now returns 404. Is DELETE idempotent here?
options: No: the second call returned a different status code
Yes: the item ends up gone either way, and the end state is what counts
No: only methods that change nothing on the server, like GET, are idempotent
Yes, because DELETE is a safe method
why: Idempotent means repeating a request leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. The responses may differ: the first DELETE removes the item, the second finds nothing, and either way the item is gone.
wrong: Idempotency is about the effect on the server, not about getting identical responses.
That describes safe methods. PUT and DELETE change data and are still idempotent.
DELETE is not safe, since it changes data. Safe and idempotent are different properties.

q: Dana is logged in with a valid token, but she is not an admin. She calls GET /admin/reports. Which response fits?
options: 401 Unauthorized, because she lacks the admin rights
200 OK with an empty report, so the client does not break
400 Bad Request, because the request asks for too much
403 Forbidden, since she is identified but not allowed
why: The server knows who Dana is; she is just not allowed to see this. That is 403. 401 is for a request with missing or invalid credentials, where logging in again could help.
wrong: Despite its name, 401 means the server could not identify the caller. Dana's token is valid.
A 200 tells the client it may see the reports and there are none. That hides a permission problem as success.
The request is well-formed. Nothing about its syntax or fields needs fixing.

q: A request has valid JSON and every required field. While saving it, a bug in the server code throws an exception. Which status should the client get?
options: 400 Bad Request, since this request is what triggered the error
404 Not Found, since the record was never saved
500 Internal Server Error, since the server's code failed
503 Service Unavailable, since the save did not go through
why: 4xx codes say the client must change something. 5xx codes say the server failed. Here the request is fine and the server's own code broke, so 500 is the honest answer.
wrong: Nothing in the request is wrong, so a 400 would send the client looking for a problem that is not there.
404 means the URL does not point to anything. The endpoint exists and was reached.
503 means the server is overloaded or down for maintenance and should be tried later. This is a bug.

q: An API allows 100 requests per minute per key. One key sends its 101st request within the minute. Which response fits best?
options: 503 Service Unavailable, since the server will not serve it now
429 Too Many Requests, ideally with a Retry-After header
403 Forbidden, since this key may not use the API
400 Bad Request, since the request breaks the API's rules
why: 429 tells this one client it is sending too fast, and Retry-After can say when to try again. The request itself is fine and the server is healthy for everyone else.
wrong: 503 says the server cannot serve anyone right now. Here only one key went over its limit.
403 means the caller is not allowed at all. This key is allowed again once the minute is over.
The request is well-formed. The problem is how many requests came, not what this one says.

q: The browser already has logo.png cached with the ETag "v42". After this exchange, what does it show?
code:
GET /logo.png HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example
If-None-Match: "v42"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "v42"
options: Its cached copy, since the image was not sent again
A broken image, since the 304 response has no body
The image from a new URL, since 3xx codes are redirects
A fresh copy, after a second GET for the full image
why: If-None-Match asks the server to send the image only if it changed since version "v42". 304 Not Modified means it has not, so no body is sent and the browser uses the copy it already holds. That saves the download.
wrong: An empty body is the point of 304. The content is already in the browser's cache.
304 belongs to the 3xx class but redirects nowhere. It has no Location and means "use your copy".
No second request is needed. The 304 already confirms the cached copy is current.

q: POST /users creates a new user, and the server gives it id 42. Which response fits best?
options: 200 OK with an empty body, since the request worked as intended
204 No Content, since the client already knows what it sent
302 Found, sending the client on to /users/42 to read the user
201 Created, with a Location header for /users/42
why: 201 says a new resource was created, and the Location header tells the client where it lives. The client needs that, because the server picked the id.
wrong: 200 only says the request succeeded. With an empty body the client never learns the new id.
The client does not know the id the server chose, and 204 has no body to carry it.
302 is a redirect for a resource found elsewhere. It does not report that something was created.

q: Which request best follows REST style for deleting order 7?
options: DELETE /orders/7
GET /orders/7/delete
POST /deleteOrder?id=7
DELETE /orders with the body {"id": 7}
why: In REST the URL names the resource and the HTTP method says what to do with it. /orders/7 is order 7, and DELETE is the action, so no verb belongs in the path.
wrong: GET must not change anything. Browsers and crawlers may follow such a link on their own.
That puts the action in the URL, RPC style. In REST the method carries the action.
DELETE /orders targets the whole collection. The order to delete belongs in the URL.

q: User 42 has a name, an email and a phone number. A settings screen changes only the email and sends just that field. Which request fits?
options: PUT /users/42 with only {"email": "new@mail.example"}
POST /users with {"email": "new@mail.example"}
PATCH /users/42 with {"email": "new@mail.example"}
GET /users/42?email=new@mail.example
why: PATCH applies a partial change to a resource, so the fields that are not mentioned stay as they are. PUT is meant to replace the whole resource with the body it carries.
wrong: PUT replaces the user with what it receives. A body with only the email may wipe the name and phone.
POST /users creates a new user. It does not update user 42.
GET must not change data, and the email would end up in logs and history as part of the URL.

q: Ana and Ben both open version 3 of a wiki page. Ana saves, making version 4. Ben then saves his edit, still based on version 3. Which response fits Ben's save?
options: 200 OK, saving Ben's page over Ana's, since the last write should win
400 Bad Request
500 Internal Server Error
409 Conflict, so Ben can review Ana's changes first
why: Ben's request is valid, but it clashes with the page's current state: saving it would silently erase Ana's work. 409 tells the client about the clash so it can fetch the latest version and merge.
wrong: Accepting it loses Ana's edit without anyone noticing, the classic lost update.
Ben's request is well-formed. A minute earlier the same request would have been accepted.
Nothing failed on the server. It detected a conflict between two users on purpose.

q: HTTP is stateless. After Maya logs in, how does the server know that her next request comes from her?
options: It recognizes her TCP connection, which stays open for the whole visit
It knows her by her IP address, which belongs to her alone
A cookie holding a session id, which the browser sends back each time
It assumes each request comes from whoever sent the request just before
why: At login the server stores a session and sends its id in a cookie. The browser attaches that cookie to every later request to the same site, so the server can look the session up and know who is asking.
wrong: Connections close and reopen during a visit, and one connection is not a user identity.
Many users can share one public IP, and one user's IP can change. It does not identify a person.
A server handles many users at once. Without a cookie or token, requests carry no link to each other.

q: A user reports a stolen laptop, and support must end that login right away. Which setup makes this easiest?
options: Server-side sessions: delete the session record on the server
Self-contained signed tokens: withdraw the token's signature
Either one: deleting the cookie in the user's other browser ends every login
Either one: changing the password cancels both kinds by itself
why: With server-side sessions every request is checked against the stored session, so deleting it ends the login on the next request. A self-contained token is checked only by its signature, so it keeps working until it expires unless the server adds a block list.
wrong: A signature cannot be withdrawn. The server would need extra state, such as a block list, to reject that token.
Deleting the cookie in your own browser does nothing to the copy on the stolen laptop.
Only if the server is built to check that. Existing sessions and tokens stay valid otherwise.

q: A session cookie is set with the HttpOnly attribute. What does that protect against?
options: Anyone on the network reading the cookie, since HttpOnly encrypts it
The cookie going out over plain HTTP instead of HTTPS
A script injected into the page reading the cookie and leaking it
Other websites receiving the cookie when the user visits them
why: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript on the page. If an attacker manages to inject a script (XSS), that script cannot read the session id and send it away. The browser still sends the cookie with requests as usual.
wrong: HttpOnly does not encrypt anything. HTTPS protects the cookie on the network.
That is the Secure attribute. HttpOnly is about scripts, not about the protocol.
A browser never sends a site's cookie to unrelated sites anyway. HttpOnly is about script access.

q: On cafe Wi-Fi you log in to https://mail.example and read your inbox. What can the cafe's network owner still learn?
options: Nothing: HTTPS hides the whole connection, even where it goes
Your password, since login forms are sent before encryption starts
The emails you read, but not what you type
That you visited mail.example, and about how much data moved
why: HTTPS encrypts what is inside the connection: URL paths, form fields, pages and cookies. It does not hide that you connected to that server's address, the site name is usually visible too, and so are the timing and size of the traffic.
wrong: The server's IP address must stay visible for packets to be routed, and the site name usually is too.
TLS is set up before the first HTTP request, so the login form is sent encrypted.
Encryption covers both directions. Pages you receive are as protected as what you send.

q: A phishing site at examp1e-bank-login.example shows a padlock in the address bar. What does the padlock tell you?
options: The connection is encrypted to whoever controls that domain name
The site is run by a verified company that has been checked as trustworthy
The browser scanned the site and found no malware on it
The real bank approved this domain as one of its own
why: The padlock means the server proved, with a certificate, that it controls the domain shown, and that traffic is encrypted. Anyone who owns a look-alike domain can get such a certificate, so the padlock says nothing about honesty.
wrong: Basic certificates only prove control of the domain name. They say nothing about who runs the site.
The padlock is about the connection, not a malware check of the site's content.
The certificate covers the look-alike name its owner registered. The real bank had no say in it.

q: On airport Wi-Fi your bank's site shows a full-page certificate warning. What is the safest way to read it?
options: The bank's server is down and this is an old copy
The site uses older encryption that is slower but still safe
The server could not prove it owns the bank's name; someone may be in between
The certificate is a formality, so clicking through keeps exactly the same protection
why: Encryption only helps if you are talking to the right server. The certificate is how the server proves it owns the name. If that check fails, an attacker on the network could be posing as the bank, so you should not continue.
wrong: A server that is down gives a connection error, not a certificate warning.
The warning is about who the server is, not about the strength of the encryption.
Without a valid certificate you could have an encrypted connection to an attacker, which protects nothing.
